checks.claim: Bates spent nearly eleven years in the Amazon collecting mostly insects
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'nearly eleven years on the Amazon' (1848-1859); over 14,700 species, mostly insects. Grokipedia gives 1848-1859.

checks.claim: Models: boldly patterned, foul-tasting butterflies of one group (heliconids) that birds leave alone
checks.note: Grokipedia: Heliconius 'unpalatable due to toxic compounds', warning patterns deter birds; Wikipedia: Bates never saw the slow-flying Heliconidae 'persecuted by birds'.

checks.claim: Mimics: a few edible butterflies of a quite different family (pierids, Leptalis/Dismorphia)
checks.note: Wikipedia: pierid mimics (Leptalis, now Dismorphia), a different family, scarce and edible ('a scarce, edible species takes on the appearance of an abundant, noxious species').

checks.claim: Key: birds that learned to shun the foul kind shun the look-alikes too
checks.note: Predators learn to avoid the model after a bad experience and 'extend this aversion to the similar-looking mimic' (Grokipedia, Henry_Walter_Bates page); Wikipedia: Bates supposed predators learn to avoid the noxious species.

checks.claim: Wrong: birds sickened give up eating butterflies
checks.note: Avoidance is of the pattern; Bates's pierids of other patterns were 'much persecuted'. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: birds startled by the pattern let them go
checks.note: Batesian protection is learned aversion, not startle; wrong in this case.

checks.claim: Wrong: birds cannot pick them out among bright flowers
checks.note: Warning patterns are conspicuous, the opposite of crypsis; wrong.

checks.claim: Context: mimicry of colouring is a structural adaptation
checks.note: School resources class camouflage and mimicry (colour pattern) as structural/physical adaptations; some note mimicry can have a behavioural side (Bates's mimics also flew like the models), but 'a structural adaptation of colouring' is standard usage.

checks.claim: Context: works only while look-alikes stay rarer than the foul kind
checks.note: Grokipedia: works 'only when mimics remain rarer than models'; Wikipedia: mimics generally less numerous, frequency-dependent selection. A fair 8th-grade simplification.

checks.claim: Scarlet kingsnakes harmless; red, yellow and black rings like the venomous coral snake
Pfennig's team set out 1,200 plasticine snakes in the Carolinas
checks.note: The 1,200 models (ScienceDaily, Scientific American) cover the whole study, Arizona included. The Nature letter (Pfennig, Harcombe & Pfennig 2001, 410:323; methods as quoted in search snippets of nature.com/articles/35066628.pdf) put 10 triplets at 8 sympatric + 8 allopatric sites in North and South Carolina = 480 replicas (25, 5.2%, attacked), and the Arizona part used 14 + 10 sites = 720 replicas (49, 6.8%, attacked): 480 + 720 = 1,200. Fix: 'set out hundreds of plasticine snakes in the Carolinas' (or '480'), or keep 1,200 and drop 'in the Carolinas' (e.g. 'set out 1,200 plasticine snakes, most of them in Arizona and the rest in the Carolinas' is overlong; 'hundreds' is simplest).

checks.claim: Models ringed like kingsnakes, others striped or plain brown; bite marks recorded attacks
checks.note: Controls had stripes instead of rings, or plain brown; plasticine kept bite and scratch marks.

checks.claim: Some inside coral snake range, some farther north where none live
checks.note: Southern NC and SC inside the range; central NC north of it.

checks.claim: Key: rings protect only where coral snakes live
checks.note: Pfennig: predators 'readily attacked our model scarlet king snakes, but only where no coral snakes lived'; Nature: predators avoid mimics only in sympatry with the model.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: protect wherever kingsnakes live / draw attacks where coral snakes live / make no difference
checks.note: Mimics attacked more in allopatry than sympatry, so all three are wrong.

checks.claim: Context: about 6 percent of attacks on ringed models where coral snakes live, about half farther north
checks.note: Pfennig's press figures 'about 50 percent vs. about 6 percent'; UNC Endeavors describes the measure as the share of all attacks falling on kingsnake replicas (one third if random), matching the context's wording.

checks.claim: DeVries went to Antarctica in 1961 as a graduate student
checks.note: Scientia: 13 months at McMurdo in 1961, from Stanford; NSF: antifreeze discovered in fish he collected at McMurdo 'while he was a graduate student at Stanford University in the early 1960s'.

checks.claim: Seawater about -1.9 C, cold enough to freeze most fishes' blood
checks.note: Seawater about -1.9 C (1969 paper: -1.87 C); temperate fish would freeze at about -0.8 C.

checks.claim: With Wohlschlag: salts and small substances explained only about half; a carbohydrate-containing protein much of the rest
checks.note: DeVries & Wohlschlag, Science 163:1073 (1969): NaCl, urea and free amino acids explained only about half of the freezing-point depression; a carbohydrate-containing protein accounted for about 30 percent (of the whole), i.e. most of the remainder.

checks.claim: Key: binds to tiny ice crystals and stops them growing
checks.note: Grokipedia: AFPs act by 'binding to ice crystals and inhibiting their growth'.

checks.claim: Wrong: makes heat / freeze solid and thaw / stops seawater soaking in
checks.note: AFPs work by ice binding, not heat or a barrier; freeze tolerance is a different strategy (wood frog).

checks.claim: Context: ice crystals enter with food and through gills; physiological adaptation; wood frog freezes and thaws
checks.note: Scientia: ice enters through feeding or gills; Kesler TEKS 8.13C guide lists antifreeze proteins in polar fish as physiological; Grokipedia: wood frog 65-70% of body water frozen, revives on thawing.
